summary: This proposed standard specifies a DNS resource record for use with the Host Identity Protocol. The record lets a HIP node store in DNS its Host Identity, the public part of its key pair, and its Host Identity Tag, a hash of that key, along with rendezvous server info.

eli5.summary: This defines a phone-book entry in DNS for a computer using HIP. It holds the computer's public key information so others can look it up.

questions: what is the hip dns resource record
what does the hip rr contain
how do i find a hip host rendezvous server in dns
is the hip rr safe without dnssec
subtitle: A DNS record type that publishes a HIP host's public key, its tag and its rendezvous servers.

tldr.problem: A HIP Initiator needs the Responder's Host Identity and Host Identity Tag before it starts the base exchange, and needs the name of its rendezvous server if the host moves around. Ordinary DNS records only hold IP addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The HIP resource record (DNS type 55) stores a public key algorithm, the HIT, the public key (the Host Identity) and optionally the domain names of rendezvous servers in preference order.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8005 obsoletes RFC 5205 and adds ECDSA keys among other clarifications. The RR gives no trust by itself: the RFC says to fetch it over a secure channel such as DNSSEC and to authenticate peers by their HI, not just the HIT.

today: RFC 8005 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5205, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It pairs with the rendezvous extension in RFC 8004.

sections.title: Why HIP Needs a DNS Record
sections.content:
Applications usually turn a domain name into IP addresses with a DNS lookup. With HIP, IP addresses are meant mostly for on-the-wire delivery, while upper-layer protocols and applications use Host Identities (HIs) or Host Identity Tags (HITs). So a way to turn a name into an HI is needed, and the RFC defines a HIP resource record for it.

The HIP base exchange (RFC 7401) is a four-way handshake of I1, R1, I2 and R2 packets. These packets contain both HITs, so the Initiator must know the Responder's HI and HIT before sending the I1. And since the rendezvous extension (RFC 8004) lets an Initiator send its I1 to a server instead of the Responder, the record also names the Responder's rendezvous servers.
sections.eli5: To write to someone, you need their name, their lock and where to send the mail. This record puts the lock and the forwarding desk into the phone book.

sections.title: Looking Up a HIP Host
sections.content:
An Initiator that starts with HIP records queries the Responder's name with type HIP. If the answer has RCODE=3 (Name Error), the host's information is not in the DNS and further queries for that name SHOULD NOT be made. If the answer has RCODE=0 and an empty answer section, there is no HIP information, and an Initiator whose policy allows falling back to opportunistic HIP or plain IP then asks for A and AAAA records.

For a static single-homed host, the HIP answer carries the HIT and HI, and the A or AAAA queries return its addresses. For a mobile host, the HIP answer also carries an RVS domain name such as rvs.example.com, whose A or AAAA records give the RVS address. The Initiator sends its I1 to the RVS, which relays it to the mobile node.

HIP RRs carry a TTL. Once the seconds since retrieval exceed it, the record MUST be treated as invalid and deleted, and a fresh query MUST be made if the record is needed. With multiple HIP RRs at one name, how a host picks between them is out of scope, but it MUST check that the RVS used is associated with the HI being used.
sections.eli5: You look the name up in the phone book. If there is no entry, you either try the old way or give up. If the friend moves a lot, the entry points to a forwarding desk.

sections.title: What the Record Stores
sections.content:
A HIP RR can hold a node's HI (its public key), the associated HIT, and the names of its possible rendezvous servers. A host MUST always calculate the HI-derived HIT itself for use in the exchange, as RFC 7401 specifies. The HIT in the record SHOULD only serve as an optimization, such as a table lookup.

The Rendezvous Server field may include the record's own owner name, which is equivalent to listing no RVS. That happens when the host is mobile and its A or AAAA records point at its RVS, or when it is stationary and reachable directly, a degenerate case where the host acts as an RVS for itself.

The HIP RR is class independent.
sections.eli5: The entry holds the public lock, a short nickname for it, and optionally the forwarding desks. Your computer should always work out the nickname itself instead of just trusting the one in the book.

sections.title: The HIP RR Wire and Text Formats
sections.content:
The RDATA has these fields: an 8-bit HIT length (in bytes), an 8-bit PK algorithm, a 16-bit PK length (in bytes, network byte order), the HIT as a binary value, the Public Key, and optionally one or more Rendezvous Servers. The first five are REQUIRED; the server field is OPTIONAL.

PK algorithm values reuse the IPSECKEY RR algorithm types: 1 for DSA, 2 for RSA, and 3 for ECDSA, which this document adds. Rendezvous servers are uncompressed wire-encoded domain names, concatenated, whose zero-length terminating label separates them. They are listed in order of preference within one RR, but that order MUST NOT be used to compare servers stored in different RRs.

In a zone file, the HIT length and PK length are not written. The HIT is Base16 and the public key is Base64, each with no whitespace, followed by the server names separated by whitespace.
sections.eli5: The entry is a form with boxes in a fixed order: how long the nickname is, which kind of lock, the lock itself, and then any forwarding desks in order of favorite.

sections.title: Zone File Examples
sections.content: The RFC gives three examples for www.example.com. using algorithm 2 and the same HIT and key: one with no RVS, one with rvs.example.com., and one with both rvs1.example.com. and rvs2.example.com.. The record's presentation form is written as IN HIP ( pk-algorithm base16-encoded-hit base64-encoded-public-key rendezvous-server... ).
sections.eli5: The examples show the same phone-book entry with no forwarding desk, one desk, or two.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The HIP RR gives two peers each other's public keying material, so, like the IPSECKEY RR, it is exposed to attacks on unsecured records. A HIP node SHOULD obtain HIP RRs from a trusted party over a secure channel, and DNSSEC provides one. DNSSEC only guarantees integrity and authenticity between the zone's DNS server and the node. It does not show that the zone publisher is trusted, so the RRSIG of the HIP RRSet MUST NOT be taken as a certificate binding the HI or HIT to the owner name.

Without a secure channel, an attacker who tampers with the record, for example by DNS spoofing, can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on the HIP exchange, or redirect I1 packets by changing the RVS name for denial-of-service or man-in-the-middle attacks. Combining both lets the attacker sit in the middle, and then HIP gives neither confidentiality nor protection of the Initiator's HI from eavesdroppers.

Secure hashes such as SHA1, which HIP uses to derive a HIT, may eventually become insecure. So an implementation SHOULD NOT authenticate peers based solely on a HIT retrieved from the DNS, but SHOULD use HI-based authentication. Without DNSSEC, the record is exposed to the threats in RFC 3833.
sections.eli5: If a trickster can change the phone book, they can swap in their own lock. So you should check the book is genuine and never trust the short nickname alone.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: RFC 5205 registered the HIP resource record type as value 55, and references now point to this document. The document reuses the IPSECKEY algorithm types, with 1 for DSA and 2 for RSA shown for reference. IANA made one new assignment in the IPSECKEY algorithm registry: value 3 for an ECDSA key.
sections.eli5: The HIP entry keeps its official number, 55, and a new key kind gets number 3.
